messages.subject_clean: [poppr] Population labels VCF import
messages.body_plain:
Hi, If you have the population data in a separate table/spreadsheet, you can import that spreadsheet into a data frame using read.table() and then add it to your data set using the strata() function.

An example workflow might go something like this, assuming you have two files: a VCF file and a csv file containing columns for individual, population, and subpopulation:

# load the libraries -----------------------------------------

library("vcfR")
library("poppr")

# read in the data -------------------------------------------

dat      <- read.vcfR("myvcf.vcf")
mystrata <- read.csv("popsubpop.csv")

# Convert to genclone and add the strata ---------------------

dat.gc         <- as.genclone(vcfR2genind(dat))
sampleorder    <- match(indNames(dat.gc), mystrata$individual)
strata(dat.gc) <- mystrata[sampleorder, ] # make sure the samples are ordered correctly
setPop(dat.gc) <- ~population             # set the population factor

You can also look at the strata tutorial about what the strata represents: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/wiki/Tutorials

Hope that helps,
Zhian

Postdoctoral Researcher (Everhart Lab)
Department of Plant Pathology

Hello,

I think I know why you were having this problem:

1. You didn't have anything defined in your strata [1].
2. You didn't have a variable called "pop" defined in your workspace
3. Pegas saw a variable called "pop", which was a function, and gave a warning ("elements in the rhs of the formula are not all factors")

However, given your code below, I'm not exactly sure why it works because "popslot" is not the same as "popslot_Kob". This tells me that you may run into problems in the future.

You can define your strata with a data frame where each row represents a sample and each column is a different population grouping. A simple way to define it for the population:

strata(Kob_snpclo) <-  data.frame(population = pop(Kob_snpclo))

>From there, you would use "population" on the right hand side of the formula in AMOVA.

Cheers,
Zhian

[1]: If you are unfamiliar with strata, check out the strata tutorial: https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/wiki/Tutorials

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

rogers.dist is basically a scaled Euclidean distance (Equation 8 of Rogers 1972) whereas diss.dist/prevosti.dist/bitwise.dist* returns the fraction of dissimilar sites, but is not euclidean. The advantage of measuring the fraction of dissimilar sites is that the results are easily interpretable, but at the cost of applicability to more geometric analyses.

Rogers, J S. 1972. Measures of genetic similarity and genetic distances.
Pages 145–153 of: Studies in Genetics. University of Texas Publishers.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

*This comes up a lot, but bitwise.dist is no different than diss.dist or Provosti's distance. The purpose of its design is simply to handle genlight objects more efficiently, but will have no qualitative difference than these other distances.

messages.subject_clean: [poppr] bruvo.dist by pops?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The error you are getting is due to the fact that genind2genpop() converts your genind object to a genpop object.

There is currently no *automated* way of performing this operation since Bruvo's distance was only designed for individuals.  Moreover, to complicate matters, the data is internally transformed to a different format (called "bruvomat"). Basically, you're going to have to roll your own.

My recommendation would be to use the boot.phylo() function in ape with a "bootgen" object (use new("bootgen", mydata) for that [1]) and a custom function that will:

1. convert your bootgen object to a genind object
2. feed it into Bruvo's distance
3. calculate the average distance between populations
4. create a tree from this distance

A couple of things you should consider:

A. You will need to make sure your data is coded in repeat lengths, not fragment lengths. One way bootgen objects work is by not particularly caring what the names of the loci are, but this has the side effect of being useless for Bruvo's distance on observed fragment lengths.
B. I do not know how one would deal with within-population variance when calculating population-level distances from an individual distance.

At some point in the future, I will add a way to calculate Bruvo's distance directly on a matrix/data frame but that day hasn't come yet.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

[1]: https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/reference/coercion-methods.html

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

> I understand that mlg.filter collapses mlgs into clonal lineages based on genetic distances but does it get rid of the clones as well?

No. It does not remove clones, it provides multilocus lineage assignment for each sample. You must use clone-correction if you want to have one representative sample per multilocus lineage.

> Also how do you propose to do the linkage disequlibrium analysis and AMOVA and other structure analysis using contracted genotypes?

The AMOVA function in poppr already has a method of performing analysis on filtered data. The only drawback is that you are then unable to assess error from within-individual variance if you don't have haploids. https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/reference/poppr.amova.html

If you have an analysis that uses a distance matrix, you can obtain that from the mlg.filter() function by setting stats = "DISTANCES" (https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/reference/mlg.filter.html). This will give you a distance matrix for the collapsed multilocus lineages.

For other analyses, you may want to run clone-correction on shuffled data sets to get a sense of the variability. I would caution against using clone-correction for linkage analyses unless you have a large sample size after clone-correction as these are known to result in non-significant values of linkage (https://zkamvar.github.io/dissertation/5-factors-influencing-inference-of-clonality-in-diploid-populations.html#fig:sim4).

> Earlier, people used to publish results original and clone corrected data for comparison.
> How should I report results with filtered mlgs? Do I report it with original data or do I report it after clone correction of the filtered mlg data?

I would recommend to be as transparent as possible. Be sure to report the distance metric, threshold, and algorithm used to define the MLLs. The multilocus lineages are most useful for reporting genotypic diversity statistics such as those produced by the poppr() function.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

Greetings,

I have SSR data set with hybrid individuals of varying ploidy (2-12). As such, I have been using the bruvo.boot() function to try and compare the data. The data set consists of a set of SSR markers that have a 3 nucleotide motif however alleles have been observed within the set that differ by less than 3 nucleotides. Additionally, some of the alleles are true null alleles and have been coded as zeros. When running the data set with the individuals with null alleles I receive the following error:

Error in hclust(DD, method = method, ...) :
  NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 11)

If I remove the individuals that are null at these markers the function runs fine and no error is produced.

Is there a recommended way to code these individuals to handle the possibility of null alleles?

My initial thought is to code the allele as either 001 or 999. For example, a tetraploid individual with a null allele the coding would be 001/001/001/001 or 999/999/999/999

Is this an appropriate way to treat the problem?

Jason

Hello,

The error is coming from the presence of missing data in your distance matrix due to randomly sampling entirely null alleles for an individual. In cases like this, use the ape function "njs" as the tree parameter.

Regarding null alleles, yes, coding them as 999 or 001 should give you the effect that the distance for individuals with null alleles will be 1 at that locus. However, this is a bit of a hack since these alleles do not fit within the stepwise mutation framework and the result would be increased genetic distances at these individuals, so you will want to check for clustering by the presence of null alleles.

Hope that helps,
Zhian

As you are a beginner, I would recommend using RStudio projects as well (https://support.rstudio.com/hc/en-us/articles/200526207-Using-Projects).

Zhian

I want to make a note of a couple of things here to help encourage best practices:

1. getfile() allows you to browse for your files, but it's not very good for reproducible practices because you have to interactively run it.
2. system.file() is only for example data files. This is a common mis-conception because it's named terribly. A better replacement is file.path().
3. I see that you are installing from github. This may be risky because that is a development version. It's better to use install.packages() with CRAN.
